html:
A Step-by-Step Compliance Checklist for Industries (2026)

With enforcement tightening across India, one of the most common reasons industries fail environmental inspections is improper vendor verification. Many facilities install Retrofit Emission Control Devices (RECDs) believing they are compliant-only to discover during inspection that the vendor’s approval cannot be verified.

This guide explains exactly how industries should verify CPCB-approved RECD vendors in India, using the same checks followed by regulators and State Pollution Control Boards.

If your DG sets are above 125 kVA, this verification process is no longer optional-it is critical for compliance.

Why Vendor Verification Matters More Than Installation

A common misconception is that any RECD installation automatically ensures CPCB compliance. In reality, regulators do not evaluate compliance based on the presence of a device alone.

During inspections, authorities verify:

  • Vendor credibility
  • Technology approval
  • Document traceability

If a vendor fails verification, the installation may be rejected-even if emission reduction appears visually effective.

This is why the CPCB Approved Vendor Network & Compliance framework places such strong emphasis on verification, not just procurement.

First: Understand What “CPCB Approved” Really Means

The Central Pollution Control Board does not issue marketing certificates or public vendor rankings. Instead, CPCB approval works through:

  • Technology performance testing
  • Acceptance of test reports
  • Regulatory alignment during inspections

So when a vendor claims “CPCB approved,” industries must verify the basis of that claim, not accept it at face value.

Step-by-Step: How to Verify CPCB Approved RECD Vendors

Step 1: Ask for Technology Test Reports (Not Just Certificates)

Start by requesting:

  • Emission test reports for the RECD
  • Proof of ≥70% particulate matter (PM) reduction
  • Load-based performance data

These reports should reference:

  • CPCB testing protocols
  • Recognised automotive or emissions testing laboratories

🚩 Red flag: Vendors who provide only brochures or self-declared compliance letters.

Step 2: Check the Testing Authority’s Credibility

Valid RECD test reports are usually issued by:

  • Government-recognised testing agencies
  • Automotive research or emission certification labs
  • CPCB-referenced or SPCB-accepted facilities

If the testing agency itself is not recognized, the report may not be accepted during inspection.

Step 3: Verify Capacity Matching With Your DG Set

Approval is capacity-specific.

Ensure the RECD:

  • Is tested for your DG set’s kVA range
  • Matches engine type and exhaust characteristics
  • Is approved for continuous or intermittent use (as applicable)

An RECD tested on a smaller DG set cannot automatically be used on a higher-capacity generator.

Step 4: Request Installation & Commissioning Records

Regulators often ask:

  • When was the RECD installed?
  • Who installed it?
  • Was commissioning done as per guidelines?

A compliant vendor should provide:

  • Installation certificates
  • Commissioning checklists
  • Photographic or technical records

This documentation proves that compliance is implemented, not theoretical.

Step 5: Verify Traceability of the Vendor

During inspections, authorities check:

  • Vendor company name
  • GST and business registration
  • Manufacturer or system integrator details

Why this matters:

  • If documentation cannot be traced back to a legitimate vendor, compliance may be questioned.
  • Fly-by-night vendors often disappear after installation, leaving industries exposed.

Step 6: Confirm SPCB Acceptance History (If Available)

While CPCB sets standards, inspections are conducted by State Pollution Control Boards.

Ask vendors:

  • Where has this RECD been installed earlier?
  • Has it been accepted during SPCB inspections?
  • Can references be shared?

Vendors with a proven acceptance history are far safer choices.

Step 7: Evaluate Inspection & Audit Support Capability

Compliance does not end after installation.

A CPCB-aligned vendor should:

  • Support during inspections
  • Help respond to notices or clarifications
  • Provide updated documents if norms evolve

This is a major advantage of working within a structured CPCB Approved Vendor Network & Compliance system, rather than relying on isolated suppliers.

Common Vendor Verification Mistakes Industries Make

Even experienced facilities fall into these traps:

  • Accepting “CPCB approved” claims without documents
  • Verifying only price, not approval basis
  • Ignoring capacity-specific testing
  • Skipping installation documentation
  • Choosing vendors who vanish after commissioning

Each of these can lead to inspection failure-even after significant investment.

How Regulators Actually Verify Vendors During Inspections

During site visits, inspectors typically:

  • Review RECD test reports
  • Match vendor names across documents
  • Check DG capacity vs RECD rating
  • Verify installation records
  • Assess maintenance readiness

If inconsistencies appear, authorities may:

  • Issue show-cause notices
  • Impose penalties
  • Restrict generator operation

This is why verification before installation is far safer than post-inspection explanations.

Vendor Verification Is a Compliance Strategy, Not a Formailty

In 2026 and beyond, CPCB compliance is no longer about ticking boxes. It is about:

  • Evidence
  • Traceability
  • Regulatory confidence

Industries that follow a structured verification process:

  • Avoid penalties
  • Reduce downtime risk
  • Build long-term regulatory trust

Key Takeaway: Verify First, Install Second

To summarise:

  • CPCB does not publish a simple vendor list
  • Vendor approval must be verified through documents
  • Testing, capacity matching, and traceability are critical
  • SPCB acceptance matters in real-world enforcement
  • CPCB-aligned vendor networks offer the safest path to compliance
